severity_definitions.hard_fail: Only corruption, unsafe publication, false evidence, wrong-domain routing, secret exposure, broken required journeys, nondeterministic governed output, or executable failure.
severity_definitions.strong_warning: Repairable page defects, administrative drift, or a quality issue needing attention. Never blocks by itself.
severity_definitions.soft_warning: Word-count targets, optional metadata, cadence variance, low cache hit rate, and editorial preferences.
severity_definitions.self_repair: Generated daily pages receive one deterministic mechanical repair pass and one final audit. No recursive repair loops.

severity_matrix_policy.note: A validator absent from severity_matrix is treated as HARD_FAIL. Failing safe matters more than convenience: an unclassified check is one nobody has reasoned about.
severity_matrix_policy.strict_flag: --strict promotes STRONG_WARNING and SOFT_WARNING failures to blocking.

validators.rationale: False evidence, already named in severity_policy. Every published page states that affiliated citations carry rel="sponsored nofollow". Nothing verified it: validate_brand_link_concentration.py uses the sponsored token to select commercial links, so a link that lost its rel drops out of the concentration count instead of being reported, and the aggregate looks better for the defect. The only tool that could see it, backfill_rel_attributes.py, had no caller. This is that same scan run as a check: it fails if any absolute link to a domain in data/brands.json is missing either token. It measures 0 missing across 632 pages today, so blocking cannot regress a clean surface.

Wrong-domain routing and false evidence, both already named in severity_policy. Every daily page states that this publication cites affiliated projects 'where the citation is topically relevant'. Across 598 affiliated placements that was false for about 39%: 82 sat outside their target's declared clusters, 105 pointed at targets that declared no clusters at all, and 46 at hosts the pantry did not recognise. uscisexam.com, the one property in the portfolio earning AI citations, was cited from a page about trauma-informed leadership; dentistryguides.com from a page about credit-report errors. A disclosure that does not describe what the page does is worse than none, because it is read as proof. This blocks on an undeclared target, on a declaration written in clusters the publication does not use, on an affiliated placement outside its target's scope, and on build_brief() failing to decline - so a clean corpus cannot be produced by a generator whose two permissive fallbacks have been restored.
Wrong-domain routing: a placeholder, missing, shared or cross-publication analytics id sends one publication's reader data into another's project.

False evidence about whether publishing is governed. data/cadence/policy.json declared 3 new pages per week and scripts/cadence_gate.js enforced it, while the autopilot published 9 a day - 63 a week, 21x the cap - and never met the gate, because git-auto-commit-action pushes with GITHUB_TOKEN and GitHub does not trigger workflows on those pushes. The cap was written down, validated, and structurally unreachable by the only process that could break it. This blocks if the generator stops consulting the declared allowance, applies it after generating rather than before, lets it exceed the cap, or stops reporting a zero-page day as the ordinary success it is.
False evidence: verifies each published backlink actually resolves.

False evidence at generation time. portfolio_backlink_engine.py seed rewrote all 32 seed pages from the bare render() template on every run, deleting the outbound citations that later lanes had added, and reported "pages": [] while doing it. That is what regressed the citation floor to founder 86 / memphis 85 / professional 382 in run 33650439764. This reads the generator's own plan_seed_writes() rather than a second copy of the rule and fails if any planned write would drop a citation, hard-failing when the planner returns nothing or when none of the planned pages is on disk. Catching this one lane later, at external_citation_coverage, is catching it after the auto-commit step could have published the loss.

False evidence, already named in severity_policy. Every page states that this publication cites affiliated projects where the citation is topically relevant, which reads as an occasional editorial choice. On 2026-08-28 approval-prep was cited from 290 of professional-resources' 420 pages - 69%, and 292 of the network's 490 commercial links - while the leading brand in the other two publications sat at 31.4% and 32.7%. Every one of those links carried rel="sponsored nofollow" and was inside its declared topical scope, so no existing validator could see it: each placement was individually correct and the aggregate was the defect. The disclosure being accurate made it worse, not better. This blocks on a brand over the declared third of any publication, on the cap being removed or raised in content-bank/scaling-policy.json, on the scheduler no longer withholding slots from a brand at its cap, on the per-brand APPROVAL_PREP_PAGES_PER_DAY bypass returning, and on any priority lane regaining a daily quota with no until_rendered_coverage to stop at.

A second way for a post to leave is a second way to burn the account, and this one cannot be seen from a configuration file. X's own API is pay-per-use and unfunded, so it is off and contacted zero times; Buffer carries the same posts to the same X profile for nothing, declared as platforms.x.delivery_route in data/social-brand-policy.json. Four things must hold and none of them is visible in a diff. The route must never exceed the ceiling BUFFER ITSELF reports at runtime from dailyPostingLimits -- a hardcoded number stays wrong after Buffer changes it -- and this repository's own X_DAILY_LIMIT must still cap a generous Buffer. It must spend that budget on ATTEMPTS, charged before the request is made and measured from inside the call, because caps that counted successes are exactly why 581 requests left this repository in 76 seconds on 2026-08-29. It must halt on the FIRST refusal and have no path back into the loop, while deferring the entries it did not carry rather than retiring them. And a post Buffer accepted must never also appear on reports/social-drafts.md, nor may the route take a post already sitting unposted on an open batch there -- either way she posts it by hand and Buffer posts it again, two identical posts on one profile. Alongside those: the queue is never consumed, queued-in-Buffer is recorded as 'buffer_queued' with its Buffer post id rather than as published, an unusable route falls back to the hand-post sheet with a named reason instead of silently ending X's distribution, X's own API is contacted zero times through every path, and BUFFER_ACCESS_TOKEN never reaches a log, a report, a sheet or a commit -- the publisher prints its report into the workflow log and commits it. Every property is driven through the real publisher with only Buffer's transport stubbed, and every one is proved negatively by running the opposite configuration. It fails if it exercises zero properties.
Cache corruption would serve wrong bytes for governed output.

A gate that cannot hold a verdict is false evidence about whether publishing is governed at all. cadence_gate.js used to rewrite the ledger it reads, so a blocked run cleared itself on the next invocation - observed as BLOCKED then CLEAR with nothing changed between them. That made the weekly publishing cap unenforceable while still reporting a status, which is worse than having no cap, because the green run was taken as proof. This blocks on the gate mutating its ledger, on two identical runs disagreeing, on no workflow invoking the gate, and on CI being able to run the acceptance path.
False evidence in the citation control plane.
False evidence. Self-reports hard/strong/soft counts.

False evidence, in the same shape as selfheal_wiring: a stage that is invoked, reports nothing, and is read as having measured something. scripts/llm_citation_probe.mjs is the only thing here that observes whether answer engines cite these publications, and it was wired into the autopilot explicitly because it had shipped in seven repositories with no caller. It was then invoked and still took no observation: loadQueries() falls back to data/seo/priority_queries.json when the config names no file, that path has never existed in this repository, an empty list exits 1 with 'no queries found', and the step is continue-on-error - so every scheduled run ended with the probe dead and the workflow green, while the step's own comment stated that observation was now being taken. The 37 queries it needed were in data/queries/evidence/evidence_queries.json, generated from the topic map for exactly this measurement, with nothing joining the two. This drives the real probe in dry-run - no key, no network, no spend - and blocks if the configured queries file is missing or empty, if the probe exits non-zero, or if it reports zero queries ready. It measures 25 ready today, so blocking cannot regress a clean surface.

Broken required journeys. Orphan count correlates inversely with AI citations across the 9 measured properties: the most-cited property carries 3 orphans and every zero-citation property is heavily orphaned. All three publications currently measure 0 orphans at a maximum depth of 2, so blocking cannot regress a clean surface - it only stops the daily generator from silently reintroducing pages nothing links to.

A page that carries no direct answer, no query-bearing h1, an empty table cell, or no outbound editorial link cannot be quoted by an answer engine or returns nothing when it is. All four checks measure 100% across the 495 published pages, so blocking cannot regress a clean surface.
Nondeterministic governed output, named verbatim in severity_policy.
Post-publish observation. Passes today with 0 verified citations, so it measures reach rather than correctness, and depends on secrets that are absent in local runs.

Corruption of published assets, and the check that caught run 33650439764. Measured 2026-08-27, all three publications together cited zero domains outside the portfolio across 608 pages: a publication that cites nobody reads as a link surface, not as reference material. Outbound citations are silent to lose -- a rebuild that drops the citation block, a source leaving the registry, a generator that stops calling add_external_citations.py -- and no other check sees any of them. data/external-citation-floor.json ratchets what each publication currently achieves and this fails if any lane falls below it, cites an unregistered domain, or marks an editorial citation rel="sponsored nofollow", which is a false paid-placement disclosure. It refuses to report PASS on an empty page loop. It measures founder 94/94, memphis 92/92, professional 399/399 today, so blocking cannot regress a clean surface.

False evidence. These publications now cite 34 outside domains, and the whole value of that is that the citations are real. This check fails if a registered source has no verification receipt, if its last fetch was not a 200, or if a citation's host disagrees with its registered domain. A fabricated government URL on a publication whose only asset is credibility is the worst failure available here, so it blocks. The network fetch is a separate opt-in flag; the blocking run is structural and offline.
Unsafe publication; already separates advisory fit notes from failures.

Broken required journeys. Every internal link in the markup the reader actually receives must resolve to a URL this build publishes. It reads the received markup rather than the tree, because the defect that took the whole network down on 2026-09-03 was injected after the origin: Cloudflare Email Address Obfuscation rewrote the governance footer's mailto: anchor into /cdn-cgi/l/email-protection, which the origin 404s, putting one broken link on every one of the 631 published pages and dropping Ahrefs site health to 4, 13 and 12 with 423, 107 and 107 errors. Nothing in sites/ was wrong, so a static link check found nothing and would have reported PASS throughout the outage. It fails if it examined zero pages, zero internal links or zero email anchors.

Two failures, either of which is unrecoverable and both of which are invisible in a diff. First, SENDING: pitches go out in the owner's name as a genuine expert, so an auto-sent pitch carrying one wrong fact gets printed under her name -- a correction in a real publication and a source relationship burned permanently and silently -- against an upside of about thirty seconds. There is therefore no send path, and this validator blocks the day one appears, including the day someone adds it for a good reason, because a good reason is exactly how it would arrive. It also requires the mailbox read to stay read-only. Second, INVENTING: a model handed a reporter's question and asked to write as an expert produces a confident answer whether or not the person has any first-hand knowledge, and the reporter cannot tell. So a draft may only use facts from data/journalist-queries/expertise-ledger.json, every fact must point at evidence that exists in this repository, and every number in a draft must appear in a fact the draft cited. The real verify_draft() is driven through a clean draft and six broken ones on every run. Beyond those it blocks if a recorded digest is marked as sent, if a recorded draft stops verifying against the ledger, if a query matching a hard exclusion reaches a model, or -- the quiet killer -- if a digest the parser cannot read is reported as 'no relevant queries' rather than as UNPARSEABLE_DIGEST, which is how a lane like this goes dead while still reporting green every morning. It fails if it exercises zero properties. It now also drives the REAL 2026-09-02 SOS digest, kept verbatim-but-redacted as a fixture. That property exists because every parser check before it used a fixture this repository wrote, so the grammar had never met its actual input -- and the first real digest parsed 2 of its 10 queries and paired query 1's summary with query 6's email address, which would have handed the owner a draft answering one reporter and addressed to another. PARTIAL_DIGEST_PARSE caught it and the run stayed green, which is the only reason eight queries were not lost silently. The expected result is derived from the message itself -- the index markers the newsletter prints and the summary/address pairs read out of the raw text -- and not from the grammar, so the grammar cannot mark its own homework.
Malformed JSON is corruption; every downstream registry reads it.
Broken required journeys and wrong-domain routing.

Broken required journeys, and the one shape of that this gate could not see. build_site_navigation.py renders bounded navigation blocks - twelve siblings, twelve recent pages - and 3ce3dbb gave it an assertion that refused to write any page that lost a link. A bounded window over a growing library has to evict, so from the day both landed, every autopilot run that actually published something aborted the rebuild and left the new pages orphaned; run 33101813017 on 2026-08-27 is the first. Neither script is wrong alone and both pass on the committed tree, which is exactly why nothing here caught it: no check ran the workflow's own order, publish then rebuild. This one does, against a temporary copy with a synthetic new daily page in it, and requires the rebuild to complete, no eviction to leave a page unreached, and click depth to still measure zero orphans. It also fails if the fixture stops evicting anything, because a guard that no longer exercises its case is not a guard.

A lane whose only consumer will never consume it. Until 2026-08-29 a run that could not post to X wrote the day's highest-value posts to reports/social-drafts.md for the owner to paste in herself and mark done with one field in data/social-draft-ledger.json. Shown what that asked of her she said "this means i manually have to do it? i will never do it honestly", so every run was producing a standing instruction that would never be followed -- worse than none, because the report kept presenting a growing pile of posts as pending work. Buffer carries the same posts to the same X profile from a free plan for nothing, so the manual lane was DELETED rather than left dormant, and this validator keeps it deleted. It drives the real publisher with Buffer's transport stubbed and every network path counted, and blocks if the retired files are back in the tree or still imported, if any run writes a sheet for a person to act on (watched at the directory level, not by trusting a path constant), if any surface instructs the owner to post or to mark anything, if the report stops counting what the route could not carry, if the free plan's standing queue-depth allowance is exceeded or is found by being refused at it rather than discovered before the request, if that depth is not read from Buffer at runtime, if a post the route could not take is dropped, retired or parked anywhere instead of staying queued_for_auto_post and going out on the NEXT run (proved across two consecutive runs against the same queue), if a post at or before marked_posted_through is sent again or that record is rewritten, if a post drafted and never posted is held back from Buffer, if X's own pay-per-use API is contacted even once, or if switching the route off resurrects a manual lane rather than leaving the entries to wait. It fails if it exercises zero properties.
Unsafe publication: page audit over changed output.
Unsafe publication: full page audit. Self-reports hard/strong/soft counts.
Unsafe publication: page audit over release output.
Wrong-domain routing and affiliation-disclosure integrity across 476 published backlinks.
Unclassified; treated as the fail-safe default.
Compile failure is executable failure.
Backfill and self-heal accounting is administrative drift; a gap is repairable and does not make published output wrong.

Executable failure, one step earlier. Seven scripts under scripts/ had no caller at all and nothing said so: three citation measurement tools and four one-shot backfills. A filename grep found the docstring that named the script and the README paragraph that described it, so each read as wired, and 'is this still reachable' had to be re-answered by hand every time. Two had rotted unnoticed while unreachable - measure_internal_reachability.py read sites/ from an absolute path outside this checkout, so a run from a worktree measured a different tree, then crashed writing its result into a scratch directory belonging to a session that no longer existed. An unreachable script is untested by everything, including this validation, while still looking live. This blocks on any tracked script under scripts/ that no runner invokes and no source imports, counts only invocations and real imports rather than prose mentions, excludes itself from its own reference corpus, and fails if it ever examines zero scripts.

A repair loop that runs green and repairs nothing is worse than no loop, because the green run is taken as proof the tree is healthy. Four such defects were reproduced on 2026-08-29: portfolio_backlink_engine.repair() gated on two lifecycle stages the 613-row registry has never held, so it matched 0 rows and printed PASS; the same function recorded findings it has no handler for as repaired; cache.fingerprint() omitted allow_repair, so a --no-repair result satisfied a repairing run and suppressed the repair; and heal_until_clean.py declared `page_validation.py changed` as a repair when that invocation cannot mutate the tree at all. This blocks on the repair gate matching zero rows, on the gate reaching withdrawn or off-topic-removed rows a prior remediation cleaned, on a claimed finding having no handler, on allow_repair leaving the cache key, on a declared repair being inert, and on no workflow invoking the loop.

Unsafe publication to live accounts, and the shape of it no configuration check can see. On 2026-08-29 the publisher made 581 requests to X in 76 seconds against X_DAILY_LIMIT=8, SOCIAL_RUN_LIMIT=3 and a jittered 90-second interval. Every one of those numbers was declared, in band, and validated by validate_social_rate_limits.py, which passed throughout - all three were counted against SUCCESSES, and X answered 402 then 429, so no counter ever moved and the loop walked the whole queue at full speed, continuing for 481 attempts after the platform had said stop. Then, because a failed attempt was stamped post_failed and no postable set contains that status, all 581 entries left the queue permanently: the X backlog went 581 to zero in one run, with the workflow green and the report calling it 'partial_failure'. A cap that only holds when nothing is going wrong is not a cap, and a guard that reads the number instead of exercising it cannot tell the difference. This drives the real publisher against a synthetic queue with the platform stubbed and blocks if a per-run slice bounds successes rather than requests, if a platform-level refusal does not stop the run, if spacing is keyed on successes, if a failing run retires the entries it could not post, if a day's scheduled runs can exceed the daily cap, if a run with zero successes reports itself as partial, or if the committed queue still carries the status the defect stamped. It fails if it exercises zero scenarios.
Declares missing_secrets_nonblocking_by_default and strict_social_failure_opt_in - non-blocking by its own contract.

Measured opportunity that produces nothing, silently. The autopilot published up to 12 pages a day and then enqueued social distribution with published[:LINKEDIN_DAILY_LIMIT] and x_pool[:X_DAILY_LIMIT]; because x_pool was built item-outer/template-inner, all 5 X slots went to published[0]. Exactly one page a day reached the queue on either platform and 428 of 474 published pages were never queued at all - not deferred, not logged, not visible in any report. Daily platform rate limits remain enforced in scripts/social_publisher.py, which leaves unposted items queued_for_auto_post so they roll to the next run: a cap that defers is fine, a cap that drops is not. This blocks if an enqueue-time slice is reintroduced, or if any governed run publishes pages that never enter the queue.

Distribution ending as a side effect of a billing decision, which no configuration check can see. X's API is pay-per-use with no free tier: every write this repository has ever made answered HTTP 402 problems/credits-depleted, starting with the very first request, and at about $0.20 per link post eight a day is roughly $48/month. On 2026-08-29 the owner declined to fund it -- "im not funding X so find a $0 workaround or kill it" -- so X is switched off. But X is off for a different reason than LinkedIn, which is off because nothing is wanted from it, and one `enabled: false` cannot hold both meanings. Draft every paused platform and LinkedIn starts producing work the owner said she did not want; draft none of them and X -- the only platform with any distribution left -- silently stops distributing while the run still exits 0 and the report still says "paused". So the pause declares its mode in data/social-brand-policy.json: "dormant" produces nothing at all, "draft_by_hand" keeps the API off while the day's posts go out by hand from reports/social-drafts.md. This drives the real publisher with post_item, both platform senders and urlopen all stubbed and counted, and blocks if a platform paused for posting produces no drafts, if it makes a single API request (no probe, no one attempt to see whether credits came back -- every one is billable), if a dormant pause produces drafts or requests, if flipping pause_mode to dormant does not stop the drafts (which would prove the mode decorative), if setting only `enabled` back to true fails to restore posting on either platform in either mode, if a paused platform is declared without a recognised pause_mode, if pausing consumes or per-row-stamps data/social-queue.json, or if the two pauses read identically in the report. It fails if it exercises zero properties.

Unsafe publication to live accounts: multiple postable entries for one page and platform is duplicate posting, the exact pattern platform spam scoring targets, and it spends the daily budget on repetition instead of reach.

Unsafe publication to live accounts: a daily limit outside the safe band either risks irreversible suspension of the X/LinkedIn accounts the authority network depends on, or restores a cap so low the queue never drains, which is a silent decision not to distribute.

A YMYL page whose entries a language model writes. The lane publishes a dated record of what changed on the USCIS filing-fee and form-edition pages, and the plan it comes from warns twice that a stale or wrong entry here is a harmful one. Two different things can put an unsupported sentence on that page: the model, which produces a fluent claim about a fee or an edition date that was never in the diff, and a person, who opens data/uscis-changelog/entries.json or the HTML and improves a headline or tidies a quote. scripts/uscis_changelog.py catches the first at write time; nothing catches the second, because no run happened. So this validator re-derives the check offline against the evidence stored with each entry -- every quoted line must appear verbatim in that entry's own stored added or removed lines -- and a hand edit fails exactly the way a hallucination does. It also blocks if an entry exists in the data file but not on the published page, if a published entry omits the agency URL or the date it was checked, if any entry's prose crosses the publication's advice boundary, if a tracked source is not registered and HTTP-200 verified in data/external-sources.json, if a snapshot's stored sha256 does not match its stored lines, or if a source that has never been successfully reached is not shown as such on the page -- that last one being how a changelog goes silently stale while its own green receipt says it is healthy. The real verify() is driven through a clean synthetic entry and five broken ones on EVERY run, including weeks with no entries, so a green receipt is never an empty loop. It fails if it examines zero items.

False evidence about the evidence itself. Every result in the receipt carried one field named `severity`, set from this matrix regardless of outcome, so 37 of 41 PASSing checks in a green release receipt read "severity": "HARD_FAIL" next to "status": "PASS", "hard_failures": 0. Run 33650439764 had exactly one real failure, external_citation_coverage; triaging that receipt for HARD_FAIL returned the whole profile and three passing validators were reported as failing. A failure marker that matches every check identifies none of them, and this is the receipt every future failure in this lane is diagnosed from. The guard reads scripts/validate.py's own classify() rather than a second copy of the rule, rejects the ambiguous key names coming back, requires every check in every profile to be classified deliberately, and re-runs generate_validation_matrix.py in a sandbox to prove the published portfolio matrix is not a stale snapshot -- that generator has never had a caller in any profile. It hard-fails when it examines zero checks.

False evidence in owner-facing published numbers. The Memphis wedding cost dataset is quoted as fact on live pages and carries the 21 verified vendor sources that most of the memphis lane's outbound citation coverage rests on; an unverified or drifted figure is a claim the publication cannot support and takes the citation floor with it.

Workflow safety: a broken trace means release automation cannot be reasoned about. It also carries the plumbing contract for the two citation lanes (journalist query scan, USCIS changelog), which is what turned them red on 2026-09-02 while both lanes themselves worked. Two distinct defects, both guarded here. First, a COMMIT PATHSPEC THAT CAN MATCH NOTHING: git-auto-commit-action exits 128 on it, and the journalist lane's pattern named an empty digests directory, so the designed, correct, most common outcome of that lane -- a day with nothing worth surfacing -- turned the workflow red. Every pathspec on both lanes is now checked against git ls-files. Second, TWO LANES PUSHING TO MAIN WITHOUT A SHARED CONCURRENCY GROUP: git-auto-commit-action does not rebase, so dispatching both at once produced a non-fast-forward push and a red run on a lane that had done its work perfectly. Both must declare the same group with cancel-in-progress false. It also blocks continue-on-error and '|| true' on those lanes, because a legitimate named stop must be green on purpose and never green by suppression. It fails if it examined zero commit pathspecs.
